cards.title: A picnic that works for everyone
cards.meaning: A story about friends planning a picnic and helping one another.
paragraphs: A picnic is more fun when friends plan ahead and help each other. Our picnic near the lake on Sunday is a good example.
First, a clear plan helps us prepare. We are going to meet at ten. I am going to bring sandwiches, Lina can bring fruit, and Omar can bring water. Everyone knows what to do.
Second, helping each other makes the work easier. Omar has a heavy bag, so we take turns carrying it. After lunch, we all help to clean up.
Planning and helping make our picnic a good day for everyone. We enjoy our food and our time together. Next time, we want to work together again.
cards.exercise: How do the friends help Omar?
cards.answer: They take turns carrying his heavy bag.
cards.example: We use “A picnic that works for everyone” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: Introduce two reasons. Explain planning with an example. Explain helping with an example. Restate both reasons.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.

cards.title: Growing something together
cards.meaning: How a community garden teaches neighbours to share responsibility and follow through.
paragraphs: A community garden needs more than seeds and tools. Our neighbourhood project showed that sharing responsibility and communicating clearly help people work well together.

First, dividing the work gives everyone a way to contribute. We started small: two neighbours brought tools, while others bought seeds. We also worked out a watering schedule so that the garden was never just one person’s responsibility.

Second, clear communication helps a group solve problems. When someone forgot to water the plants, we checked the schedule together. We made the instructions clearer instead of blaming the person, so everyone could follow through.

The garden taught us two useful lessons: share the work fairly and discuss problems openly. These habits helped our plants grow and made us a stronger team. Other community projects can benefit from the same approach.
cards.exercise: Why did the neighbours make the instructions clearer?
cards.answer: Someone had forgotten a task, so clearer instructions could help everyone understand their responsibilities.
cards.example: We use “Growing something together” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: Claim: teamwork needs shared duties and clear communication. Develop each reason with a garden example. Reconnect both reasons to the claim.

cards.title: A good plan makes room for people
cards.meaning: How clear planning and practical flexibility help people collaborate confidently.
paragraphs: A good collaborative plan should provide direction while leaving room for change. Preparing a small exhibition at our neighbourhood library taught us that shared priorities and practical testing make this balance possible.

First, agreeing on constraints gives a team a useful starting point. With a narrow room and a modest budget, we mapped out the visitor’s journey before choosing displays. This shared reference point helped us decide which ideas were workable.

Second, testing a plan makes flexibility practical. Our trial run revealed that the entrance would become crowded. We moved the introductory panel further inside, solving the problem before it required a costly last-minute change.

Effective coordination therefore combines clear priorities with opportunities to adjust. By making decisions visible and checking in before the deadline, a team can remain organised without becoming rigid. That is what makes a plan work for people.
cards.exercise: What did the trial run reveal, and how did the team respond?
cards.answer: It revealed that the entrance would become crowded. The team moved the introductory panel further inside.
cards.example: We use “A good plan makes room for people” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: Thesis: direction plus flexibility. Body 1: shared priorities, with a planning example. Body 2: testing, with a revision example. Conclude by connecting both.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.

cards.title: interdependence
cards.meaning: A situation in which people or things depend on one another.
cards.example: The project’s interdependence made isolated planning ineffective.
cards.conversation:
A: Why did one delay affect three teams?
B: The level of interdependence was higher than we realised.
A: Would separate deadlines help?
B: Only if we also made the dependencies explicit.
cards.exercise: Complete: Their mutual reliance reflects a high degree of ____.
cards.answer: interdependence
cards.wordForms: Usually uncountable: interdependence; no regular plural in this sense.
cards.synonymNote: These describe reliance in both directions.
cards.notes: Usually uncountable. Interdependence between teams means one team's decisions can affect another's work.

cards.title: reconcile
cards.meaning: To make apparently conflicting ideas, needs, or demands compatible.
cards.example: We must reconcile creative ambition with the available time.
cards.conversation:
A: Can we preserve the idea and meet the deadline?
B: We need to reconcile those competing demands.
A: Which part of the design is essential?
B: The accessible route matters more than the extra display.
cards.exercise: Complete: We must ____ ambition with available time.
cards.answer: reconcile
cards.wordForms: reconcile · reconciles · reconciled · reconciled · reconciling (base · third person · past · past participle · -ing)
cards.synonymNote: These apply to the sense of reconciling competing ideas or demands.
cards.notes: Use reconcile one demand with another. This sense concerns compatibility, not necessarily repairing a personal relationship.

cards.title: account for
cards.meaning: To take a relevant factor into consideration.
cards.example: The timeline should account for feedback from volunteers.
cards.conversation:
A: Is the schedule realistic?
B: Only if it accounts for the review process.
A: Could we shorten the review?
B: Perhaps, but we should not remove the people it is meant to include.
cards.exercise: Rewrite: “Include accessibility needs in the plan.”
cards.answer: Account for accessibility needs in the plan.
cards.notes: Here account for means allow for something in planning. In another context, it can mean explain a cause.

cards.title: build on
cards.meaning: To use an existing achievement, idea, or resource as a basis for further development.
cards.example: The revised proposal builds on what residents told us.
cards.conversation:
A: Are we discarding the first draft?
B: No. We are building on its strongest ideas.
A: Which element is worth keeping?
B: The visitor feedback gives us a strong starting point.
cards.exercise: Complete: The proposal builds ____ earlier feedback.
cards.answer: on
cards.notes: Build on feedback or experience. The expression stresses continuity rather than replacing everything that came before.

cards.title: see the wood for the trees
cards.meaning: To recognise the overall situation without becoming distracted by details.
cards.example: We were so focused on wording that we could not see the wood for the trees.
cards.conversation:
A: Are these tiny edits helping?
B: Perhaps we need to step back and see the wood for the trees.
A: What is the exhibition meant to achieve?
B: It should help residents see their experiences represented.
cards.exercise: What is the equivalent American expression?
cards.answer: See the forest for the trees.
cards.notes: Usually found with can't or couldn't. This is the British form; American English commonly uses forest instead of wood.

cards.title: meet halfway
cards.meaning: To reach a compromise in which both sides make concessions.
cards.example: Both teams agreed to meet halfway on the format.
cards.conversation:
A: They want a long report, but we prefer a short one.
B: Could we meet halfway with a summary and an appendix?
A: Would both teams accept that?
B: They might, provided the appendix remains easy to find.
cards.exercise: Suggest a compromise using “meet halfway”.
cards.answer: We could meet halfway by keeping the summary short and adding an appendix.
cards.notes: It need not mean a mathematically equal split. The emphasis is on reciprocal willingness to adjust.

cards.title: Before we optimise the process, let’s clarify its purpose.
cards.meaning: A reminder to establish what a process is for before trying to make it more efficient.
cards.example: Before we optimise the process, let’s clarify its purpose.
cards.conversation:
A: Could we make the review faster?
B: Yes, but first let’s clarify what it is intended to achieve.
A: What is the review supposed to protect?
B: Accuracy, accessibility, and the chance to challenge assumptions.
cards.exercise: Paraphrase “clarify its purpose”.
cards.answer: Make clear what it is meant to achieve.
synonyms: Let’s establish the goal before improving the method.
First ask what the procedure is meant to achieve.
cards.notes: Optimise concerns how well a process works; clarify its purpose asks whether the intended goal is understood.

cards.title: Less is more.
cards.meaning: A simple choice can be more effective than adding many things.
cards.example: We choose two useful decorations and leave the rest of the table clear.

B: “Less is more.”
A: How does that connect with the example?
B: The example removes unnecessary additions so that the useful choices stand out.
cards.exercise: Explain how the example illustrates the quoted idea. Which detail supports your explanation?
cards.answer: The example removes unnecessary additions so that the useful choices stand out.

cards.title: Although / despite
cards.meaning: Use although before a clause, and despite before a noun phrase or an -ing form, to express contrast.
cards.example: Although time was limited, we tested the plan. Despite the time limit, we tested it.
cards.conversation:
A: Did the constraints stop the trial?
B: No. Despite having little time, we completed it.
A: Did the consultation change the plan?
B: Yes. We revised the entrance and simplified the labels.
cards.exercise: Rewrite with “despite”: Although the budget was limited, we consulted residents.
cards.answer: Despite the limited budget, we consulted residents.
cards.notes: Although the budget was limited; despite the limited budget; despite having little time. Do not write despite of.

cards.title: Has this changed the way you approach teamwork?
cards.meaning: A reflective question about whether an experience has influenced someone's way of collaborating.
cards.example: Has this project changed the way you approach teamwork?
cards.conversation:
A: Has this changed the way you approach teamwork?
B: Yes. I now ask about expectations much earlier.
A: Which expectations would you ask about first?
B: Who can decide, who should be consulted, and what success means.
cards.exercise: Ask a thoughtful follow-up.
cards.answer: Which expectation would you clarify first next time?
cards.notes: The present perfect connects a past experience with the person's current approach. Invite an example rather than assuming change occurred.

cards.title: Making disagreement productive
cards.meaning: Why constructive disagreement can strengthen collective judgement.
paragraphs: Collaboration gains value from constructive disagreement, not merely smooth agreement. Two conditions make dissent productive: a shared purpose that disciplines the discussion and relevant evidence that helps participants revise their views.

A shared purpose gives disagreement a useful boundary. In a community exhibition project, debates about the format initially reflected personal preferences. Once the team agreed that residents’ access mattered most, we could distinguish essential requirements from choices open to negotiation.

Evidence then turns that common purpose into better decisions. Residents’ feedback revealed that the proposed layout was difficult to navigate. This concrete finding allowed us to reconcile accessibility with creative ambitions, replacing competing tastes with a problem we could solve together.

Constructive disagreement thus depends on both common aims and a willingness to respond to evidence. Consensus is more valuable when it emerges from this inquiry. Good collaboration makes the reasoning behind agreement visible rather than treating agreement itself as proof of success.
cards.exercise: According to the essay, what makes disagreement productive?
cards.answer: A shared purpose, a distinction between requirements and preferences, and visible reasoning help turn disagreement into useful inquiry.
cards.example: We use “Making disagreement productive” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: State two conditions for productive dissent. Develop shared purpose and evidence in separate example-led paragraphs. Synthesise their contribution to sound agreement.
cards.notes: Follow the main idea through two supported points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.

cards.title: reciprocity
cards.meaning: The practice or principle of mutual exchange, response, or obligation.
cards.example: Meaningful reciprocity cannot always be reduced to an exchange of equal favours.
cards.conversation:
A: Must each contribution be identical?
B: No. Reciprocity can accommodate different capacities.
A: Does reciprocity require equal contributions?
B: Not identical ones, but some recognition of mutual obligation.
cards.exercise: Why is “reciprocity” broader than an immediate exchange?
cards.answer: It can involve mutual responsiveness over time rather than equal, immediate returns.
cards.wordForms: Usually uncountable: reciprocity; no regular plural in this sense.
cards.synonymNote: Mutuality is broader; reciprocity often involves a responding act or obligation.
cards.notes: Usually uncountable. Reciprocity need not imply identical contributions, immediate repayment, or perfectly equal power.

cards.title: circumscribe
cards.meaning: To restrict something within defined boundaries.
cards.example: The brief circumscribes the committee’s authority without dictating every decision.
cards.conversation:
A: Can the committee change the project’s purpose?
B: No. Its authority is circumscribed by the brief.
A: Would those limits prevent useful action?
B: They could clarify which decisions require wider consent.
cards.exercise: Complete: The brief ____ the committee’s authority.
cards.answer: circumscribes
cards.wordForms: circumscribe · circumscribes · circumscribed · circumscribed · circumscribing (base · third person · past · past participle · -ing)
cards.synonymNote: Delimit stresses defining boundaries; restrict stresses limiting freedom or scope.
cards.notes: A formal verb, often used of authority, discretion, or possibilities. It emphasises setting limits rather than necessarily eliminating something.

cards.title: bear on
cards.meaning: To be relevant to, or have an effect on, a matter under consideration.
cards.example: The history of the site bears directly on the proposed design.
cards.conversation:
A: Is the earlier dispute relevant?
B: Yes. It bears on how residents interpret the proposal.
A: So procedural fairness is not the whole question?
B: Correct. We must also ask whose experiences the process recognises.
cards.exercise: Rewrite with “bear on”: This evidence is relevant to our decision.
cards.answer: This evidence bears on our decision.
cards.notes: Use bear on a question, judgement, or outcome. It does not mean physically carrying something in this sense.

cards.title: hold in tension
cards.meaning: To recognise competing ideas or values without prematurely resolving or dismissing either.
cards.example: We must hold openness and accountability in tension.
cards.conversation:
A: Can one principle settle the matter?
B: Probably not. We need to hold both concerns in tension.
A: Must we choose one value over the other?
B: Not immediately; preserving the tension can improve the decision.
cards.exercise: What does this phrase suggest about conflicting values?
cards.answer: They may need to coexist without being reduced to a single simple rule.
cards.notes: Common in analytical discussion. Holding two values in tension allows their competing demands to remain visible.

cards.title: move the goalposts
cards.meaning: To change the requirements for success after a process has begun.
cards.example: Changing the criteria after submission felt like moving the goalposts.
cards.conversation:
A: The proposal met every published requirement.
B: Then adding a new condition now would move the goalposts.
A: Could the new requirement still be justified?
B: Yes, but its rationale and consequences should be made explicit.
cards.exercise: Why might this expression imply unfairness?
cards.answer: People are judged against criteria that changed after they acted.
cards.notes: Usually critical: the speaker suggests the change is unfair or makes achievement unnecessarily difficult.

cards.title: the devil is in the detail
cards.meaning: A saying that apparently minor details can determine whether a plan succeeds or creates difficulties.
cards.example: The agreement sounds fair, but the devil is in the detail.
cards.conversation:
A: Everyone supports shared ownership.
B: Yes, but the devil is in the detail: who can veto a decision?
A: Which detail could alter the outcome?
B: Who has the authority to revisit the decision.
cards.exercise: Give one detail that could complicate shared ownership.
cards.answer: The rules governing who can veto a decision.

cards.notes: Use it to direct attention to implementation. Detail is commonly singular in this established form, though details also occurs.

cards.title: Agreement is meaningful only when dissent remains possible.
cards.meaning: An agreement has substance only if people are still free to express disagreement.
cards.example: Agreement is meaningful only when dissent remains possible.
cards.conversation:
A: Nobody objected during the meeting.
B: Did everyone feel able to object?
A: Would allowing objections guarantee a sound decision?
B: No. It is a necessary condition in this claim, not a sufficient one.
cards.exercise: Paraphrase the sentence without “dissent”.
cards.answer: Agreement matters only if people are free to express disagreement.

cards.notes: Only when sets a necessary condition. It does not claim that allowing dissent is sufficient to make every agreement legitimate.

cards.title: Not until… did…
cards.meaning: After a fronted Not until phrase or clause, invert the auxiliary and subject in the main clause.
cards.example: Not until the assumptions were made explicit did the disagreement become manageable.
cards.conversation:
A: When did the discussion improve?
B: Not until we named the underlying assumptions did we make progress.
A: Why is did placed before the subject?
B: The fronted negative expression triggers inversion in the main clause.

cards.title: What assumption did the discussion leave unexamined?
cards.meaning: A question inviting scrutiny of a belief that a discussion may have taken for granted.
cards.example: What assumption did the discussion leave unexamined?
cards.conversation:
A: What assumption did the discussion leave unexamined?
B: That everyone had the same freedom to participate.
A: How might we test that assumption?
B: We could ask whose evidence or experience might challenge it.
cards.exercise: Offer a follow-up that invites nuance rather than a yes/no answer.
cards.answer: How might unequal freedom to participate have shaped the apparent consensus?
cards.notes: Unexamined does not necessarily mean false. Ask what evidence or alternative perspective might test the assumption.

cards.title: The limits of consensus
cards.meaning: An examination of the conditions under which consensus can support legitimate collective action.
paragraphs: Consensus can legitimise collective action, but unanimity alone proves little. Agreement deserves authority when participation is substantively fair and decisions remain open to revision; these conditions matter more than the appearance of complete alignment.

Fair participation requires scrutiny of how alternatives are framed. A neighbourhood committee may vote unanimously for a venue after consulting only residents who can attend evening meetings. The result appears orderly, yet excludes relevant experience. Such omissions bear on legitimacy even when formal procedures are followed.

Revisability provides a second safeguard against premature closure. The committee could circumscribe its decision-making authority, record objections and review the venue after a trial event. This approach enables action while preserving a route for overlooked needs to influence the outcome.

Legitimate consensus therefore combines inclusive deliberation with accountable revision. It holds decisiveness and openness in tension, allowing people to act together without pretending that differences have disappeared. A collective voice earns authority by remaining answerable to its constituent voices.
cards.exercise: Why does the writer distinguish unanimity from legitimate agreement?
cards.answer: Unanimity can result from deference or exclusion, so legitimacy depends on the conditions of participation and the continuing possibility of disagreement.
cards.example: We use “The limits of consensus” when we discuss this idea.
cards.structure: Qualify the claim that consensus legitimises action. Examine inclusive participation, then revisability, using a connected example. Synthesize the conditions of legitimate agreement.
